title: Breeding objectives and selection indices
text:
1. Define the breeding objective
Let \(u\) be a vector of additive breeding-value deviations on a fixed genetic base, and \(a\) a vector of marginal economic values in currency per trait unit. Define aggregate genetic merit
\[H=a^Tu.\]
Here growth and feed consumption are measured in kg over the same production period. A larger growth deviation is assigned a positive value; greater feed consumption is assigned a cost. These are hypothetical values chosen for teaching, not an economic assessment of a real enterprise.

section: 2. Specify the information used for selection

2. Specify the information used for selection
Now introduce a separate hypothetical set of measurement deviations \(x\), centered on a fixed external reference mean. These are not assumed to be the observed measurements of the preceding candidate breeding values.
Define \(P=\operatorname{Var}(x)\), \(C=\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)\) and \(G=\operatorname{Var}(u)\). Covariance matrices are supplied population moments, not estimates from four candidates. A matrix’s labels and units are part of its meaning.


Show R code

x <- rbind(A=c(growth=2,feed=1),B=c(growth=1,feed=-1),
           C=c(growth=-1,feed=-2),D=c(growth=3,feed=4))
P <- matrix(c(4,1,1,9),2,2,dimnames=list(traits,traits))
C <- diag(c(1,4)); G <- diag(c(2,5))
dimnames(C) <- dimnames(G) <- list(traits,traits)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(x),rownames(P)),
          identical(colnames(P),rownames(C)),
          identical(colnames(C),names(a)),identical(rownames(G),names(a)),

Question 2. Why is \(C\) not automatically equal to \(G\)?






Suggested answer





Measurements and breeding values are different quantities. Their cross-covariance depends on what was measured and how it relates to genetic merit. For arbitrary predictions, using genetic covariance in place of the required prediction/merit cross-covariance can double-count or misrepresent information.

title: Breeding objectives and selection indices
text:
3. Solve for a linear index
Choose \(I=b^Tx\) to minimize \(E[(H-I)^2]\) under the centered moment model. Since
\[E[(H-I)^2]=a^TGa-2b^TCa+b^TPb,\]
differentiation gives \(Pb=Ca\). With positive-definite \(P\),
\[b=P^{-1}Ca.\]
Use a linear solve rather than explicitly constructing an inverse. Economic weights \(a\) define the objective; index coefficients \(b\) account for information variance and cross-covariance.

I <- drop(x %*% b)

Question 3. Does directly applying economic weights to measurements produce the same ranking as the index?

title: Breeding objectives and selection indices
text:
4. Calculate model-based index accuracy
Under the supplied moments,
\[\operatorname{Var}(I)=b^TPb,\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(I,H)=b^TCa,\quad \operatorname{Var}(H)=a^TGa.\]
The model correlation is their covariance divided by the product of standard deviations. At the optimal index, \(\operatorname{Cov}(I,H)=\operatorname{Var}(I)\).


Show R code
VI <- drop(crossprod(b,P %*% b))
CIH <- drop(crossprod(b,C %*% a))
VH <- drop(crossprod(a,G %*% a))

  prediction_error_variance=VH-2*CIH+VI)

title: Breeding objectives and selection indices
section: 5. Predict a response under explicit selection assumptions
text:
5. Predict a response under explicit selection assumptions
For a jointly Gaussian \((x,u)\) population and upper-tail truncation on \(I\), selecting fraction \(f\) gives standardized intensity \(i=\phi(z)/f\), where \(z=\Phi^{-1}(1-f)\). The model mean breeding-value difference of selected candidates is
\[\Delta u=\frac{i\,C^Tb}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(I)}}.\]
For the optimal index, objective difference is \(\Delta H=i\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(I)}\). These distribution and selection assumptions are additional to solving the covariance equation.

Question 4. Is this automatically next-generation gain per year?






Suggested answer





No. It is the expected mean breeding-value difference of selected candidates under the model. In a simple additive, nonoverlapping-generation setting with unchanged base and no other shifts, offspring gain depends on the selected parents’ gene contributions across both roles; equal selected sire/dam means give the same predicted offspring mean difference. Annual gain additionally needs a declared generation interval. Mating, contribution limits, diversity and costs are separate decisions.

section: 4. Measure contributions and expected offspring merit
text:
4. Measure contributions and expected offspring merit
For \(N\) offspring, let \(n_j\) be the number of parental slots assigned to parent \(j\). Its fraction of transmitted genes is \(c_j=n_j/(2N)\). Sire contributions sum to one half, and dam contributions sum to one half. Under additive inheritance and mean-zero Mendelian sampling,
\[E(\overline H_{\mathrm{offspring}}\mid\mathrm{plan})
=\sum_j c_j\widehat H_j.\]
This is a prediction conditional on the supplied parental evaluations and model. If true parental merit were known, the same expression would give the conditional genetic expectation. It does not describe realized Mendelian sampling.

Question 3. Could different pairings with the same contributions change expected mean additive merit?






Suggested answer

title: Simulating selection response
section: 1. Declare the biological and programme assumptions
text:
1. Declare the biological and programme assumptions
We use 32 diploid founders, six linked biallelic markers on one chromosome, and one additive trait measured in arbitrary trait units. The genome has no dominance, mutation or migration in this example. Marker effects remain fixed. gsim models chromosome-wise meiosis with Poisson crossovers and no interference, using the supplied cumulative genetic map.
Each generation has 16 candidates per parental role. Select four sires and four dams, then draw 32 offspring by uniform independent parent sampling with replacement. Every new cohort replaces the previous cohort as the candidate population; no parents are carried over. Offspring sex alternates by identity so that role counts remain fixed. This is a deliberate programme simplification.

title: Simulating selection response
section: 2. Create a synthetic phased founder panel
text:
2. Create a synthetic phased founder panel
Use R’s RNG only to create this tiny synthetic input. Calls explicitly contain phase: 0|1 and 1|0 identify different parental copies. Here allele 1 is VCF ALT, G; gsim retains it as BIM A1 and dosage counts this allele. File outputs go to a new temporary folder on each run.


Show R code
library(gsim)
needed <- c("gsim_import_vcf","gsim_simulate_pedigree","gsim_simulate_cohort",
  "gsim_trait_state","gsim_genetic_values","gsim_records","gsim_select","gsim_mate")
stopifnot(all(needed %in% getNamespaceExports("gsim")))
work <- tempfile("selection-practical-")
dir.create(work)
ids <- sprintf("base%02d",1:32)
markers <- paste0("m",1:6)
set.seed(20261008)
h1 <- matrix(rbinom(32*6,1,.5),32,6,dimnames=list(ids,markers))
h2 <- matrix(rbinom(32*6,1,.5),32,6,dimnames=list(ids,markers))
vcf <- file.path(work,"founders.vcf")
header <- paste(c("#CHROM","POS","ID","REF","ALT","QUAL","FILTER",
                  "INFO","FORMAT",ids),collapse="\t")
body <- vapply(seq_along(markers),function(j) {
  paste(c("1",10*j,markers[j],"A","G",".",".",".","GT",
          paste(h1[,j],h2[,j],sep="|")),collapse="\t")
},character(1))
writeLines(c("##fileformat=VCFv4.2",header,body),vcf)
map <- data.frame(chromosome="1",variant_id=markers,
                  genetic_position_cm=seq(0,100,length.out=6))
reference <- gsim_import_vcf(vcf,map,file.path(work,"reference"))
parent_table <- data.frame(animal=ids,sire=NA_character_,dam=NA_character_,
                          sex=rep(c("M","F"),16),generation=1L)
pedigree0 <- gsim_pedigree_from_table(parent_table)
phase0 <- gsim_simulate_pedigree(reference,pedigree0,101,
                               file.path(work,"base-phase"),"hap")
bed0 <- gsim_simulate_pedigree(reference,pedigree0,101,
                             file.path(work,"base-dosage"),"bed")


The two founder exports use the same stored founder alleles. They provide phased input for transmission and dosage input for reporting. They do not independently redraw founders.

title: Simulating selection response
section: 3. Freeze the architecture and reporting base
text:
3. Freeze the architecture and reporting base
For dosage \(d_{ij}\) of allele G at marker \(j\), define genetic value
\[g_i=\sum_j(d_{ij}-c_j)\beta_j,\]
where effects \(\beta_j\) are in trait units per allele and centers \(c_j\) remain fixed at one. With this additive architecture, these genetic values supply the simulation’s additive merit. No cohort-specific variance normalization is applied.


Show R code
effects <- matrix(c(.2,-.1,.15,0,.05,.1),6,1,
                  dimnames=list(markers,"trait"))
state <- gsim_trait_state(effects,center=1)
g0 <- gsim_genetic_values(bed0,state)
stopifnot(max(abs(g0-drop((h1+h2-1) %*% effects)))<1e-12)
base_mean <- mean(g0)


We will also report allele frequencies and heterozygosity at these same six markers. For this tiny teaching panel, applying an identity effect matrix with zero center returns six dosage columns through the public accumulation interface. This deliberately materializes only 32 by 6 values; it is not a whole-genome extraction workflow.


Show R code
dosage_effects <- diag(length(markers))
dimnames(dosage_effects) <- list(markers,markers)
dosage_state <- gsim_trait_state(dosage_effects,center=0)
d0 <- gsim_genetic_values(bed0,dosage_state)
stopifnot(identical(dimnames(d0),dimnames(h1)),
          max(abs(d0-(h1+h2)))==0)
summarize_cohort <- function(bed,policy,generation) {
  g <- gsim_genetic_values(bed,state)
  d <- gsim_genetic_values(bed,dosage_state)
  stopifnot(all(d %in% 0:2))
  p <- colMeans(d)/2
  # A second route to the mean, independent of individual aggregation.
  mean_from_p <- sum((2*p-1)*effects[,"trait"])
  stopifnot(abs(mean(g)-mean_from_p)<1e-12)
  data.frame(policy=policy,generation=generation,mean_genetic=mean(g),
    gain=mean(g)-base_mean,genetic_variance=var(drop(g)),
    mean_HE=mean(2*p*(1-p)),mean_HO=mean(colMeans(d==1)),
    polymorphic=sum(p>0 & p<1))
}

Question 1. Why not center marker dosages separately in every generation?






Suggested answer





Using each cohort’s own mean dosage would force the cohort mean genetic value to zero and hide gain. One architecture and one reporting base let us compare genetic values over time. Marker frequencies may change; the centers used for reporting do not.

title: Simulating selection response
section: 4. Generate records, select parents and simulate offspring
text:
4. Generate records, select parents and simulate offspring
Generate one phenotype per candidate as \(y_i=g_i+e_i\), with residual variance 0.04 trait units squared and no fixed or permanent-environment contribution. Select on this observable phenotype, not hidden genetic truth. Genetic truth is read separately to evaluate outcomes after the decision.
The comparison selects parents randomly with the same role quotas. It shares founder inputs and numbered seed schedules with the phenotype strategy. Diverging selected pools and pedigrees still produce different later populations; the comparison is one illustrative realization per policy.


Show R code
run_programme <- function(policy,generations=3L) {
  current <- phase0; bed <- bed0; pedigree <- pedigree0
  animals <- ids; sex <- parent_table$sex
  history <- list(summarize_cohort(bed,policy,0))
  transitions <- list()
  for(t in seq_len(generations)) {
    g <- gsim_genetic_values(bed,state)
    records <- gsim_records(g,residual_covariance=.04,seed=200+t)
    observed <- records$records
    stopifnot(all(observed$trait=="trait"),!anyDuplicated(observed$animal))
    scores <- setNames(observed$value,observed$animal)
    selection <- if(policy=="Phenotype") {
      gsim_select(animals,c(M=4,F=4),scores=scores,method="score",strata=sex)
    } else {
      gsim_select(animals,c(M=4,F=4),method="random",strata=sex,seed=400+t)
    }
    sires <- selection$animal[selection$selected & selection$stratum=="M"]
    dams <- selection$animal[selection$selected & selection$stratum=="F"]
    children <- sprintf("g%d-%02d",t,1:32)
    mating <- gsim_mate(pedigree,sires,dams,children,seed=300+t,
      sex=setNames(rep(c("M","F"),16),children))
    plan <- mating$offspring
    # Truth evaluates the already specified parentage; it did not select parents.
    parent_expectation <- mean((g[plan$sire,"trait"]+g[plan$dam,"trait"])/2)
    next_cohort <- gsim_simulate_cohort(current,mating,seed=500+t,
      output=file.path(work,paste0(policy,"-generation",t)))
    offspring_g <- gsim_genetic_values(next_cohort,state)
    # At every marker, each parent transmits one of its two alleles.
    parental_d <- gsim_genetic_values(bed,dosage_state)
    child_d <- gsim_genetic_values(next_cohort,dosage_state)
    sire_d <- parental_d[plan$sire,,drop=FALSE]
    dam_d <- parental_d[plan$dam,,drop=FALSE]
    lower <- (sire_d==2)+(dam_d==2)
    upper <- (sire_d>0)+(dam_d>0)
    stopifnot(all(child_d>=lower & child_d<=upper),
      identical(attr(offspring_g,"trait_state_checksum"),state$checksum))
    transitions[[t]] <- data.frame(policy=policy,generation=t,
      parent_expectation=parent_expectation,offspring_mean=mean(offspring_g),
      mendelian_mean=mean(offspring_g)-parent_expectation)
    history[[t+1L]] <- summarize_cohort(next_cohort,policy,t)
    pedigree <- mating$pedigree; current <- next_cohort; bed <- next_cohort
    animals <- children; sex <- plan$sex
  }
  list(history=do.call(rbind,history),transitions=do.call(rbind,transitions))
}

Question 2. Must phenotype selection increase genetic merit in every realized generation?






Suggested answer





No. Phenotype selection uses noisy records, and finite parent use and Mendelian sampling add variation. text:
6. Read gain and diversity together
Genetic variance is the sample variance of simulated additive values in each cohort. It can change through allele-frequency shifts and associations between linked markers. Mean marker \(H_E\) measures a different aspect of variation. One marker has zero trait effect but still contributes to the marker-diversity summary.
These six synthetic markers do not estimate genome-wide diversity, effective population size or pedigree inbreeding. Neither higher gain nor a family quota alone establishes a better programme. Programme comparisons also need declared constraints, generation intervals and costs. Generations here are not calendar years.

title: Relationships, mating and inbreeding
section: 2. From parental kinship to offspring inbreeding
text:
2. From parental kinship to offspring inbreeding
For two individuals \(s,d\), kinship \(\phi_{sd}\) is the probability that one randomly drawn allele from each is identical by descent relative to the founder base. The additive relationship convention is \(A_{sd}=2\phi_{sd}\). The child’s two copies come from its parents, giving
\[F_{\mathrm{child}}=\phi_{sd}=\frac{A_{sd}}{2},
\qquad A_{\mathrm{child},\mathrm{child}}=1+F_{\mathrm{child}}.\]
Thus mating these full siblings gives offspring \(F=0.25\). Pairing candidates from the two unrelated founder families gives \(F=0\) under this pedigree model.

A founder-copy check
Label the four distinct founder copies in family A. A random allele transmitted by either sibling is marginally uniform over these copies. With independent meioses producing and transmitting the siblings’ copies, enumerate all 16 equally likely pairs. Four pairs carry the same founder-copy identity.


Show R code
copies <- c("SA-copy1","SA-copy2","DA-copy1","DA-copy2")
draws <- expand.grid(sire_copy=copies,dam_copy=copies,
                     stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
F_fullsib <- mean(draws$sire_copy==draws$dam_copy)
stopifnot(F_fullsib==.25,F_fullsib==A["M1","F1"]/2)
F_fullsib


[1] 0.25


This is a probability over possible inheritance histories, not a statement that exactly one quarter of the genome in every offspring will be autozygous. Identity by descent refers to ancestral copy identity; identical nucleotide states can occur without shared descent within the declared base.
Question 1. Why is offspring inbreeding 0.25 rather than the full-sibling relationship 0.5?






Suggested answer





The additive relationship is twice kinship. Offspring inbreeding equals parental kinship because the child’s paternal and maternal copies are drawn from the two parents. Confusing these conventions gives a factor-of-two error.

Question 2. Does the between-family plan eliminate inbreeding in every future generation?






Suggested answer





No. Offspring share ancestors and become related even when their own inbreeding is zero. Future decisions need the updated pedigree and actual contributions. A zero value for this generation does not establish a sustainable long-term programme.

section: 5. Distinguish pedigree inbreeding from marker heterozygosity
text:
5. Distinguish pedigree inbreeding from marker heterozygosity
Pedigree \(F\) is an expectation about identity by descent on the founder base. Observed marker heterozygosity is a realized genotype statistic. At a biallelic locus, the model
\[P(AB)=2p(1-p)(1-F)\]
connects them only under a specified allele-frequency and identity-by-descent model. It does not turn any observed heterozygosity deficit into a pedigree inbreeding estimate.

Inbreeding depression also requires a model beyond additive values alone. With dominance or other nonadditive effects, increased autozygosity can change expected phenotype. A genomic kernel has its own allele-frequency reference, centering and normalization; its entries need an established kinship interpretation on a declared base before applying an identity-by-descent formula. Negative centered genomic entries are not negative IBD probabilities.

1. State the prediction question first
A breeding evaluation aims to predict additive genetic merit. A phenotype includes genetic and environmental contributions. Prediction performance therefore depends on the target, the population and which information will be available when selecting animals.
For this lesson, fit a phenotype predictor using a marker-derived covariate and family labels. We deliberately simulate both genetic and shared environmental family effects. A fitted family coefficient can absorb both; it is not automatically a family breeding value.

2. Generate phenotypes and retain truth separately
For animal \(i\) in family \(f\), define
\[u_i=0.6z_i+g_f,\qquad y_i=u_i+c_f+e_i.\]
Here \(z_i\) is an observed marker-derived covariate, \(g_f\) is an additive genetic family component, \(c_f\) is a shared environmental component and \(e_i\) is individual noise. Components are independent in this synthetic model. Values are in arbitrary trait units. This is a statistical teaching model, not a simulation of phased inheritance.

title: Validating predictions and selection decisions
section: 3. Fit only on information in the training set
text:
3. Fit only on information in the training set
Use ridge regression with an intercept, standardized marker covariate and family indicator columns. The penalty is fixed at 1 before looking at validation outcomes. The intercept is unpenalized; the marker and family coefficients are penalized. This is a compact phenotype-prediction model, not REML or a genomic breeding-value estimator.
Training data determine the marker center and scale. Known family identities define columns without using outcomes. A family absent from training has a zero fitted coefficient under this model, so its predictions use the intercept and marker term.


Show R code
fit_predict <- function(train,test,lambda=1) {
  center <- mean(train$marker_covariate)
  scale <- sd(train$marker_covariate)
  stopifnot(is.finite(scale),scale>0,lambda>0)
  make_design <- function(data) {
    family_columns <- outer(data$family,families,"==")*1
    colnames(family_columns) <- families
    cbind(intercept=1,marker=(data$marker_covariate-center)/scale,
          family_columns)
  }
  Xt <- make_design(train); Xv <- make_design(test)
  penalty <- diag(c(0,rep(lambda,ncol(Xt)-1)))
  coefficient <- solve(crossprod(Xt)+penalty,crossprod(Xt,train$phenotype))
  prediction <- drop(Xv %*% coefficient)
  names(prediction) <- test$animal
  list(prediction=prediction,coefficient=coefficient,
       preprocessing=c(center=center,scale=scale))
}

  Represented=observed$within_family<=6,
  Withheld=!observed$family %in% families[1:2])

  fit_predict(observed[training,],observed[!training,]))

text:
4. Report association, error and calibration
For validation phenotypes, report correlation, root mean squared error in trait units, mean error (prediction minus observation), and the intercept/slope of the diagnostic regression \(y=\alpha+\beta\widehat y+\epsilon\).
Ideal calibration would give intercept zero and slope one in the appropriate population. Correlation can remain unchanged under a positive rescaling or constant shift. Calibration diagnostics on 16 records are descriptive and uncertain.


Show R code
metrics <- function(y,prediction) {
  calibration <- lm(y~prediction)
  c(correlation=cor(y,prediction),RMSE=sqrt(mean((prediction-y)^2)),
    mean_error=mean(prediction-y),intercept=unname(coef(calibration)[1]),
    slope=unname(coef(calibration)[2]))
}

title: Validating predictions and selection decisions
text:
5. Evaluate a selected shortlist separately
Within each validation pool, select four eligible candidates by the phenotype-prediction score. For this demonstration the pool represents one parental role, with equal intended contributions. Use IDs to break ties. Compare the shortlist’s mean true genetic merit with the whole pool and with an explicitly labelled oracle shortlist using truth.

shortlists <- do.call(rbind,lapply(names(splits),function(label) {
  test <- observed[!splits[[label]],]
  prediction <- fits[[label]]$prediction[test$animal]
  true_u <- truth[test$animal]
  selected <- order(-prediction,test$animal,method="radix")[1:4]
  oracle <- order(-true_u,test$animal,method="radix")[1:4]
  selected_mean <- mean(true_u[selected])
  oracle_mean <- mean(true_u[oracle])
  stopifnot(oracle_mean>=selected_mean-1e-12)
  data.frame(split=label,selected=4,pool_mean_truth=mean(true_u),
    selected_mean_truth=selected_mean,
    selected_difference=selected_mean-mean(true_u),
    oracle_mean_truth=oracle_mean,oracle_gap=oracle_mean-selected_mean,
    oracle_overlap=length(intersect(test$animal[selected],test$animal[oracle])))
}))

Question 2. Why can phenotype prediction reward family environmental effects?






Suggested answer





Shared family environment helps predict additional phenotypes from that same environment. It is not inherited additive merit. The family predictor can therefore improve phenotype association while ranking genetic merit imperfectly. Genetic evaluations need a model and data that distinguish genetic and environmental sources, with validation matched to their use.

title: Comparing breeding programmes
text:
2. Create one synthetic founder population
Use 24 unrelated, noninbred pedigree founders and six phased markers on one chromosome. Independent Bernoulli draws supply founder alleles; this is a toy panel, not a reconstruction of historical haplotypes. G is VCF ALT and the counted allele. Cumulative map positions are in cM; offspring meiosis uses the existing gsim Poisson no-interference model.


Show R code
library(gsim)
source("../scripts/mouse_practical_helpers.R")
work <- tempfile("programme-capstone-"); dir.create(work)
ids <- sprintf("base%02d",1:24)
markers <- paste0("m",1:6)
set.seed(20261011)
h1 <- matrix(rbinom(24*6,1,.5),24,6,dimnames=list(ids,markers))
h2 <- matrix(rbinom(24*6,1,.5),24,6,dimnames=list(ids,markers))
vcf <- file.path(work,"founders.vcf")
header <- paste(c("#CHROM","POS","ID","REF","ALT","QUAL","FILTER",
                  "INFO","FORMAT",ids),collapse="\t")
body <- vapply(seq_along(markers),function(j)
  paste(c("1",10*j,markers[j],"A","G",".",".",".","GT",
          paste(h1[,j],h2[,j],sep="|")),collapse="\t"),character(1))
writeLines(c("##fileformat=VCFv4.2",header,body),vcf)
map <- data.frame(chromosome="1",variant_id=markers,
                  genetic_position_cm=seq(0,100,length.out=6))
reference <- gsim_import_vcf(vcf,map,file.path(work,"reference"))
parent_table <- data.frame(animal=ids,sire=NA_character_,dam=NA_character_,
                          sex=rep(c("M","F"),12),generation=1L)
pedigree0 <- gsim_pedigree_from_table(parent_table)
phase0 <- gsim_simulate_pedigree(reference,pedigree0,101,
                               file.path(work,"base-phase"),"hap")
bed0 <- gsim_simulate_pedigree(reference,pedigree0,101,
                             file.path(work,"base-dosage"),"bed")
effects <- matrix(c(.2,-.1,.15,0,.05,.1),6,1,
                  dimnames=list(markers,"trait"))
state <- gsim_trait_state(effects,center=1)
dosage_effects <- diag(6); dimnames(dosage_effects) <- list(markers,markers)
dosage_state <- gsim_trait_state(dosage_effects,center=0)
g0 <- gsim_genetic_values(bed0,state)
base_mean <- mean(g0)
stopifnot(max(abs(g0-drop((h1+h2-1) %*% effects)))<1e-12)


Marker effects and dosage centers stay fixed for all programmes and runs. The founder mean is the genetic-gain reference. Pedigree inbreeding is relative to the declared unrelated-founder base. Do not re-center a selected cohort when reporting gain.

3. Define records, time and accounting assumptions
A record is \(y_{iv}=g_i+e_{iv}\), with independent residual variance 0.04 trait units squared. For \(v\) independent records, the mean has residual variance \(0.04/v\). Averaging does not eliminate an environmental effect shared across visits; our example deliberately omits that component.
Costs are hypothetical accounting units: 5 per record, 20 per selected parent per generation, and 10 per offspring. They are resource charges, not trait economic weights or estimated farm profit. Each generation lasts one assumed year, including the recording stage.


Show R code
policies <- data.frame(policy=c("One record","Two records"),visits=c(1L,2L))

years_per_generation <- 1
generations <- 2L
replicates <- 3L
policies$residual_variance_of_mean <- .04/policies$visits
policies$cost_per_generation <- 24*policies$visits*charges["record"]+
  6*charges["parent"]+24*charges["offspring"]

title: Comparing breeding programmes
text:
4. Run a small paired comparison
Three runs share this same founder panel. For each run, the two policies share numbered record, mating and meiosis seed schedules. Visit 1 has the same record and observation-unit identity under both policies, so it retains its innovation when visit 2 is added. Between runs, seeds differ. Later candidate genotypes can differ across policies because selection changes parentage.
This pairing supports a difference within each run. It does not make the three runs independent founder-population experiments, nor remove all stochastic variability from their differences.


Show R code
run_programme <- function(visits,replicate) {
  policy <- policies$policy[match(visits,policies$visits)]
  current <- phase0; bed <- bed0; pedigree <- pedigree0
  animals <- ids; sex <- parent_table$sex
  history <- list(); record_count <- 0L
  for(t in seq_len(generations)) {
    seed_base <- 10000*replicate+100*t
    g <- gsim_genetic_values(bed,state)
    record_table <- expand.grid(animal=animals,visit=seq_len(visits),
                                stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
    record_table$trait <- "trait"
    record_table$record <- paste(record_table$animal,record_table$visit,sep=":")
    record_table$observation_unit <- record_table$record
    records <- gsim_records(g,records=record_table,
                           residual_covariance=.04,seed=seed_base+1)
    # Observable records alone supply the decision score.
    scores <- tapply(records$records$value,records$records$animal,mean)
    selection <- gsim_select(animals,c(M=3,F=3),scores=scores,
                             method="score",strata=sex)
    sires <- selection$animal[selection$selected & selection$stratum=="M"]
    dams <- selection$animal[selection$selected & selection$stratum=="F"]
    children <- sprintf("g%d-%02d",t,1:24)
    mating <- gsim_mate(pedigree,sires,dams,children,seed=seed_base+2,
      sex=setNames(rep(c("M","F"),12),children))
    next_cohort <- gsim_simulate_cohort(current,mating,seed=seed_base+3,
      output=file.path(work,paste0("visits",visits,"-run",replicate,"-g",t)))
    plan <- mating$offspring
    offspring_g <- gsim_genetic_values(next_cohort,state)
    d <- gsim_genetic_values(next_cohort,dosage_state)
    p <- colMeans(d)/2
    full <- mating$pedigree$pedigree
    tab <- data.frame(id=full$animal,sire=full$sire,dam=full$dam)
    tab <- tab[match(mating$pedigree$canonical_order,tab$id),]
    A <- mouse_relationship(tab)
    offspring_F <- diag(A)[children]-1
    F_from_parents <- A[cbind(match(plan$sire,rownames(A)),
                             match(plan$dam,colnames(A)))]/2
    stopifnot(max(abs(offspring_F-F_from_parents))<1e-12,
      identical(attr(offspring_g,"trait_state_checksum"),state$checksum),
      abs(mean(offspring_g)-sum((2*p-1)*effects[,"trait"]))<1e-12)
    parent_expectation <- mean((g[plan$sire,"trait"]+g[plan$dam,"trait"])/2)
    record_count <- record_count+nrow(records$records)
    cost <- record_count*charges["record"]+t*6*charges["parent"]+
      t*24*charges["offspring"]
    history[[t]] <- data.frame(policy=policy,replicate=replicate,generation=t,
      years=t*years_per_generation,gain=mean(offspring_g)-base_mean,
      mean_F=mean(offspring_F),mean_HE=mean(2*p*(1-p)),
      records=record_count,cost=unname(cost),
      parents_used=length(mating$parents_used),
      mendelian_mean=mean(offspring_g)-parent_expectation)
    pedigree <- mating$pedigree; current <- next_cohort; bed <- next_cohort
    animals <- children; sex <- plan$sex
  }
  do.call(rbind,history)
}

  do.call(rbind,lapply(policies$visits,function(v) run_programme(v,r)))))

Question 1. Does reducing record noise guarantee more gain and less inbreeding in every run?






Suggested answer





No. Recording precision changes selection information; finite selection, mating and segregation still vary. More accurate selection does not automatically preserve diversity. With connected pedigrees, selecting more similar high-merit relatives can also affect future relationships. These outcomes need separate evaluation.

title: Comparing breeding programmes
section: 6. Make the decision conditional on resources and assumptions
text:
6. Make the decision conditional on resources and assumptions
For a hypothetical horizon budget of 1,000 accounting units, only the one-record programme is feasible under these charges. A budget of 1,200 makes both feasible. Feasibility and expected performance are different questions: an infeasible strategy is excluded by the budget, while an uncertain performance difference calls for more evidence within an agreed experimental design.
The trait objective is additive merit. Recording cost is paid by the programme. To translate gain into economic benefit, specify trait units, production volume, marginal values, timing and discounting. Subtracting these accounting costs directly from a mean genetic value would mix units.

Suggested teaching routes

Foundations of genetic variation
Read PG 1 → PG 2 → PG 3 → PG 4, then QG 1 → QG 2 → QG 12. Students move from allele coding and random-union expectations to sources of trait variation.
Checkpoint: explain why a heterozygosity deficit does not identify pedigree inbreeding, and why a locus’s dominance effect and average allele-substitution effect are different quantities.


Genetic evaluation and validation
Review PG 1–2, then work through QG 1 → QG 2 → QG 3 → QG 4 → QG 5 → QG 10. This route follows the mouse analysis and ends by examining what a validation split actually tests.
Checkpoint: distinguish predicted breeding values, phenotype predictions, model-based reliability and empirical validation. State which information is available at the prediction date and whether validation animals have relatives in training.


Population change and evolutionary selection
Work through PG 1 → PG 2 → PG 3 → PG 4 → PG 5 → PG 6 → PG 7 → PG 9. Use QG 2 as a bridge between gene action for a trait and genotype fitness.
Checkpoint: separate deterministic expectations from finite-population realizations. Fitness dominance in PG 7 is a different model quantity from phenotypic dominance in QG 2; economic weights in QG 6 describe another decision layer.


Disease alleles and phenotype probability
Review PG 2–3 → PG 13. Declare the phenotype observation window and penetrance vector before translating genotype frequencies into phenotype probabilities.
Checkpoint: state when prevalence equals q squared, and distinguish population averages, known-parent crosses and reverse conditioning.


Sequence divergence and dating
Review PG 1 → PG 4–5 → PG 12. Define the alignment denominator and substitution model before converting distance into time.
Checkpoint: distinguish a mismatch fraction from substitution distance, a per-lineage rate from a pairwise rate, and sequence common ancestry from a species split.


DNA-profile probability
Review PG 2–3 → PG 5 → PG 11. State the population and independence assumptions, then distinguish a fixed-profile probability, agreement between random profiles and a source likelihood ratio.
Checkpoint: explain why a match probability is not a posterior source probability and why shared population membership can induce dependence across loci.


Conservation management
Review PG 3–4 → PG 6 → PG 10, with QG 9 for pedigree relationships. Compare immediate offspring inbreeding, parental group coancestry and marker heterozygosity before imposing a budget.
Checkpoint: explain why equal contributions can produce different offspring inbreeding, and why a contributor concentration descriptor does not estimate effective population size.


Breeding-programme design
Review PG 3–4 and PG 6, plus the evaluation concepts in QG 3–5. Then use QG 6 → QG 7 → QG 8 → QG 9 → QG 10 → QG 11. For a shorter design session, focus on QG 6, 7, 9 and 11, reading the simulation and validation assumptions before the capstone.
Checkpoint: define the objective, candidate eligibility, information schedule, parent contributions, mating, genetic base, calendar horizon and budget before comparing outcomes. Higher score correlation alone does not select a programme.

title: Genotype-by-environment interaction and heritability
text:
1. Environmental shifts and genotype responses
A reaction norm describes how one genotype’s expected phenotype changes with environment. Parallel lines can show an environmental effect without interaction. Nonparallel lines show that the genotype contrast changes; crossing lines additionally reverse rankings. Interaction does not require a crossover.
These supplied means illustrate three patterns in arbitrary trait units. They are not observed trial data.


Show R code
patterns <- list(
  Parallel=rbind(G1=c(6,7),G2=c(5,6)),
  Nonparallel=rbind(G1=c(6,9),G2=c(5,6)),
  Crossover=rbind(G1=c(7,5),G2=c(5,7)))
for(k in seq_along(patterns)) colnames(patterns[[k]]) <- c("E1","E2")
contrasts <- lapply(patterns,function(m) m["G1",]-m["G2",])
stopifnot(identical(unname(contrasts$Parallel),c(1,1)),
          identical(unname(contrasts$Nonparallel),c(1,3)),
          identical(unname(contrasts$Crossover),c(2,-2)))

Question 1. Can an environment improve the mean trait value without changing genotype rankings?






Suggested answer





Yes. In the parallel example, both genotypes increase by one unit and their contrast remains one. In the nonparallel example, the contrast changes but G1 remains higher. Ranking reverses only in the crossover example.

title: Genotype-by-environment interaction and heritability
text:
2. Declare a replicated-genotype experiment
Imagine eight clonally replicated genotypes, each tested in three environments with four independent experimental units per genotype/environment cell. Replicates are separate units, not repeated measurements of the same plant. There are no blocks, spatial trends, missing values or shared residual effects in this teaching design.
For genotype \(i\), environment \(j\) and replicate \(k\), use
\[y_{ijk}=\mu+E_j+G_i+(GE)_{ij}+\epsilon_{ijk}.\]
Environment means \(E_j\) are fixed nuisance effects. Genotype effects have variance \(\sigma_G^2\); independent genotype/environment deviations have variance \(\sigma_{GE}^2\); independent unit residuals have variance \(\sigma_\epsilon^2\). All random components have mean zero and are mutually independent. Environments are treated as exchangeable for interaction sampling around a target mean. This covariance model is a simplification of environments with heterogeneous variances or correlated genotype responses.
The genotype component represents repeatable genetic differences between these complete genotypes. It is not automatically additive breeding value. Randomized allocation and absence of genotype-associated environmental confounding are essential to that interpretation.


Show R code
set.seed(20261012)
nG <- 8L; nEnv <- 3L; nRep <- 4L
genotypes <- paste0("G",seq_len(nG))
environments <- paste0("E",seq_len(nEnv))
truth_variance <- c(G=4,GE=2,residual=1)
g <- setNames(rnorm(nG,sd=sqrt(truth_variance["G"])),genotypes)
ge <- matrix(rnorm(nG*nEnv,sd=sqrt(truth_variance["GE"])),nG,nEnv,
             dimnames=list(genotypes,environments))
environment_mean <- setNames(c(-3,0,3),environments)
data <- expand.grid(genotype=genotypes,environment=environments,
                    replicate=seq_len(nRep),stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
data$genotype <- factor(data$genotype,levels=genotypes)
data$environment <- factor(data$environment,levels=environments)
cell <- cbind(match(data$genotype,genotypes),match(data$environment,environments))
data$value <- 20+environment_mean[as.character(data$environment)]+
  g[as.character(data$genotype)]+ge[cell]+rnorm(nrow(data),sd=1)
stopifnot(nrow(data)==96,all(table(data$genotype,data$environment)==nRep))

4. Estimate variance components from mean squares
For this balanced independent-unit model, expected mean squares are
\[E(MS_\epsilon)=\sigma_\epsilon^2,\] \[E(MS_{GE})=\sigma_\epsilon^2+n_{\mathrm{rep}}\sigma_{GE}^2,\] \[E(MS_G)=\sigma_\epsilon^2+n_{\mathrm{rep}}\sigma_{GE}^2+

title: Genotype-by-environment interaction and heritability
section: 5. Define heritability for the observation unit
text:
5. Define heritability for the observation unit
The target is a genotype’s main genetic effect across the declared environment population. The observation used to compare genotypes is its mean across \(n_{\mathrm{env}}\) environments and \(n_{\mathrm{rep}}\) units per environment. After common environment effects are accounted for, interaction and residual terms average differently:
\[H^2_{\mathrm{mean}}=
\frac{\sigma_G^2}{\sigma_G^2+
\sigma_{GE}^2/n_{\mathrm{env}}+
\sigma_\epsilon^2/(n_{\mathrm{env}}n_{\mathrm{rep}})}.\]
This balanced entry-mean definition requires the declared covariance and sampling model; see Piepho and Möhring (2007) for its distinction from unbalanced-trial measures. An entry mean and an individual phenotype are different observation units, so they need different variance denominators.

  variance["G"]/(variance["G"]+variance["GE"]/environments+
    variance["residual"]/(environments*replicates))
}

6. Broad-sense genetic differences are not additive breeding values
Complete genotypes can differ through additive, dominance and epistatic effects. This replicated-genotype design estimates repeatable genetic variation without partitioning those sources. Under an appropriate orthogonal variance decomposition, broad-sense heritability includes all genetic components; narrow-sense heritability includes only additive variance. See Practical 3 for an explicitly additive relationship model.

title: Association mapping, covariates and multiple testing
section: 1. Define the population, marker coding and phenotype model
text:
1. Define the population, marker coding and phenotype model
Use 160 independent diploid individuals in two groups, with 100 hypothetical biallelic markers. Dosage counts allele G, with A as the other allele. Marker positions and chromosome assignments are illustrative metadata, not real genomic coordinates. The genotype matrix is small enough to retain in memory.
Marker m1 contributes directly to the generating phenotype. Marker m2 has identical dosages to m1 and is a perfect tag, with no separate direct effect. Marker m3 has a large group-frequency difference but no direct effect. The groups also differ in environment, creating a path from group membership to both genotypes and phenotype.


Show R code
set.seed(20261013)
n <- 160L; m <- 100L
ids <- sprintf("animal%03d",seq_len(n))
markers <- paste0("m",seq_len(m))
group <- factor(rep(c("A","B"),each=n/2))
sex <- factor(rep(c("F","M"),n/2))
p <- runif(m,.2,.5)
M <- matrix(rbinom(n*m,2,rep(p,each=n)),n,m,dimnames=list(ids,markers))
M[,"m1"] <- rbinom(n,2,ifelse(group=="A",.2,.8))
M[,"m2"] <- M[,"m1"]
M[,"m3"] <- rbinom(n,2,ifelse(group=="A",.1,.9))
M[,"m100"] <- 0 # Invariant marker, explicitly excluded from testing.
# Phenotype is generated before introducing missing calls at another marker.
y <- 2+.8*M[,"m1"]+4*(group=="B")+.5*(sex=="F")+rnorm(n,sd=1.5)
M[sample(seq_len(n),8),"m5"] <- NA_real_
records <- data.frame(animal=ids,group=group,sex=sex,phenotype=y)
metadata <- data.frame(marker=markers,chromosome=rep(1:5,each=20),
                       position_bp=rep(seq(1000,20000,by=1000),5),
                       counted_allele="G",other_allele="A")
stopifnot(identical(records$animal,rownames(M)),
          identical(metadata$marker,colnames(M)),all(na.omit(c(M)) %in% 0:2))
knitr::kable(data.frame(marker=c("m1","m2","m3","m5","m100"),
  called=colSums(!is.na(M)) [c("m1","m2","m3","m5","m100")]),row.names=FALSE)

title: Association mapping, covariates and multiple testing
text:
2. Define the association hypothesis
For marker dosage \(d_i\), fit
\[y_i=\mu+\gamma_{\mathrm{group}(i)}+
\eta_{\mathrm{sex}(i)}+\beta d_i+\epsilon_i.\]
The marker test asks whether its regression coefficient \(\beta\) is zero conditional on the declared covariates. It is an additive dosage test with one degree of freedom. A genotype-factor test or additive-plus-dominance test is a different hypothesis. The coefficient is in trait units per counted G allele and is not a genotype’s total breeding value.
Only animals with a called marker and complete covariates/phenotype enter that marker’s regression. No imputation is used. Exclude invariant markers and rank-deficient designs before forming the tested family. Model-based t-test p-values depend on the regression assumptions; multiple-testing adjustment cannot repair confounding, correlated errors or misspecified effects. Exact Gaussian-error inference requires a correctly specified conditional mean and error model; this illustrative marginal scan is not a calibration study.


Show R code
scan_markers <- function(adjusted=TRUE,genotypes=M) {
  do.call(rbind,lapply(colnames(genotypes),function(marker) {
    dosage <- genotypes[,marker]
    use <- !is.na(dosage) & complete.cases(records)
    data <- records[use,]; data$dosage <- dosage[use]
    result <- data.frame(marker=marker,called=sum(use),
      allele_frequency=mean(data$dosage)/2,beta=NA_real_,SE=NA_real_,
      p_value=NA_real_,status="tested")
    if(length(unique(data$dosage))<2) {
      result$status <- "invariant"; return(result)
    }
    formula <- if(adjusted) phenotype~group+sex+dosage else phenotype~dosage
    X <- model.matrix(formula,data)
    if(qr(X)$rank<ncol(X) || nrow(X)<=ncol(X)) {
      result$status <- "unestimable"; return(result)
    }
    fit <- lm(formula,data=data)
    coefficient <- coef(summary(fit))["dosage",]
    result$beta <- coefficient["Estimate"]
    result$SE <- coefficient["Std. Error"]
    result$p_value <- coefficient["Pr(>|t|)"]
    result
  }))
}
unadjusted <- scan_markers(FALSE)
adjusted <- scan_markers(TRUE)
stopifnot(sum(adjusted$status=="tested")==99,

Check the covariate-adjusted coefficient independently
Residualize both phenotype and m1 dosage against the same covariates. Their residual regression slope equals the full regression’s marker coefficient. Residualizing only phenotype while leaving dosage unadjusted would not generally produce the same result.

title: Association mapping, covariates and multiple testing
text:
3. State the multiple-testing family
There are 99 estimable marker tests in this declared panel. Adjustment covers that family within the prespecified covariate-adjusted scan. The unadjusted scan is an instructional sensitivity comparison, not an additional source from which to choose the smallest p-value. If selecting discoveries across several models or traits, the testing policy must reflect those additional choices.
At a family-wise level of 0.05, Bonferroni uses a raw threshold \(0.05/99\). Holm also controls family-wise error and can be less conservative. Benjamini–Hochberg targets false discovery rate under independence or appropriate positive dependence; Benjamini–Yekutieli handles more general dependence. FDR concerns the expected false proportion among rejected hypotheses, not the probability that one particular marker is false. See the R p.adjust documentation for the supported procedures.

number_tests <- sum(valid)
for(method in c("bonferroni","holm","BH","BY")) {

}

section: 4. Plot the marker scan using aligned metadata
text:
4. Plot the marker scan using aligned metadata
Use chromosome and position only for displaying results. The synthetic panel is not a dense real genome, and the plotted threshold applies to these 99 tests rather than a universal GWAS threshold.


Show R code
stopifnot(identical(metadata$marker,adjusted$marker),
          identical(adjusted$marker,unadjusted$marker))
x <- metadata$position_bp+(metadata$chromosome-1)*22000
colors <- c("#247BA0","#86B7A3")[1+(metadata$chromosome %% 2)]
local({
  old <- par(mfrow=c(2,1)); on.exit(par(old))
  for(label in c("Unadjusted","Adjusted")) {
    results <- if(label=="Unadjusted") unadjusted else adjusted
    keep <- results$status=="tested"
    significance <- -log10(results$p_value[keep])
    plot(x[keep],significance,pch=16,col=colors[keep],xaxt="n",
      main=label,xlab="Hypothetical chromosome",ylab="-log10(p)",
      ylim=c(0,max(significance,-log10(.05/number_tests))*1.1))
    axis(1,at=(0:4)*22000+10500,labels=1:5)
    abline(h=-log10(.05/number_tests),lty=2)
    at <- match(focus,results$marker)
    text(x[at],-log10(results$p_value[at]),labels=focus,pos=3,cex=.8)
  }
})








Figure 1: Unadjusted and covariate-adjusted scans of the same synthetic panel. The dashed line is the Bonferroni threshold for the 99 estimable tests; model adjustment and multiple-testing adjustment address different problems.





Covariate adjustment changes the model and its coefficients. Multiple-testing adjustment changes the rejection rule across hypotheses. Correcting many confounded p-values does not make their interpretation causal.

title: Association mapping, covariates and multiple testing
section: 5. A linked signal is not a separate causal effect
text:
5. A linked signal is not a separate causal effect
Markers m1 and m2 have identical dosages, so their separate regressions return identical coefficients and p-values. The phenotype-generating equation names m1, but the observed marker association data alone cannot distinguish the two explanations.


Show R code
i2 <- match("m2",adjusted$marker)
stopifnot(adjusted$beta[i1]==adjusted$beta[i2],
          adjusted$p_value[i1]==adjusted$p_value[i2],
          abs(cor(M[,"m1"],M[,"m2"])^2-1)<1e-12)
joint <- model.matrix(~group+sex+M[,"m1"]+M[,"m2"],data=records)
stopifnot(qr(joint)$rank<ncol(joint))


Adding both perfectly tagged markers to one model produces a rank-deficient design. With imperfect LD, further analysis may help distinguish signals but does not itself prove biological causation. Replication, fine mapping and functional evidence address additional questions. A tagged marker can be genuinely associated even without a direct effect; calling every such signal a statistical false positive would confuse association with causality.
Question 1. Does the smallest p-value identify the largest genetic contribution?






Suggested answer





No. Significance depends on estimated effect, uncertainty, allele frequency, sample size and model. It is not the fraction of trait variance explained or evidence that a variant is causal. Single-marker effect estimates can also reflect LD and be exaggerated when selected for unusually strong discovery results.

title: Association mapping, covariates and multiple testing
section: 6. Connect to the mouse practicals and real analysis
text:
6. Connect to the mouse practicals and real analysis
Practical 2 analyzes a mouse marker with additive and dominance contrasts. Practicals 3–5 use relationships for variance estimation and genetic evaluation. The mouse population contains relatives, so this independent-individual OLS scan should not be transferred directly and treated as calibrated inference.
A real association workflow must establish phenotype and marker identity alignment, allele coding, sample inclusion, missing-call handling, covariates, relatedness/structure treatment and the testing family. Association testing and genetic prediction have different targets. Discovering significant markers does not by itself validate breeding-value predictions in a new cohort; use Practical 10 for that distinction.
